title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 3
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading test: four original passages (a village literary narrative, social science on Cairo's coffeehouses, paired humanities passages on Arabic calligraphy and natural science on the White Desert), 36 questions in 40 minutes, with a reason for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a full-length practice test for the **Reading section of the enhanced ACT**: **36 questions in 40 minutes**, four passages with 9 questions each. In the real test, **27 questions are scored** and one passage is unscored, but you will not know which one, so treat every passage as if it counts. **In this practice test, all 36 questions count.** All passages and questions are original.

rows: Humanities — paired passages A and B

items: Sit in a quiet place, put your phone away and keep scrap paper and a pencil ready.
Do the whole section in one sitting. The timer starts when you press Start and the section ends automatically after 40 minutes.
Aim for about **10 minutes per passage**: roughly 3–4 minutes to read and map it, then about 6 minutes for its 9 questions.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, guess, mark it and move on.
For the paired passages, read Passage A and answer its questions, then Passage B and its questions, and finish with the questions about both.
The score shown at the end is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score.

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative

LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is from an original short story. The narrator remembers a summer from her childhood in her grandmother's village in Upper Egypt.

[1] The pigeon tower stood at the edge of my grandmother's land, where the last row of clover gave way to the dust of the road. It was taller than our house and shaped like a sugar loaf, its mud walls studded with clay pots laid on their sides so that the birds could nest in them. From a distance it looked like something a giant had set down and forgotten. Up close it smelled of feathers, grain and old rain.

[2] I was twelve the summer my grandmother stopped climbing it. Nobody announced this. One morning she simply sat on the bench beneath the tower with the tin of grain in her lap and shook it, and the birds came down to her instead of her going up to them. She did this for a week before my mother noticed, and another week before anyone said anything. When my mother finally asked about her knees, my grandmother replied that the birds were getting lazy and needed to learn to come when they were called.

[3] I had grown up believing that the tower belonged to her the way her voice did. She knew each pair of pigeons by some mark I could never see—a grey bar on a wing, a way of landing—and she spoke to them in a low clicking language that she said she had learned from her own mother. My cousins and I were allowed to watch but not to touch. "A bird you frighten," she told us, "remembers you longer than a bird you feed."

[4] That summer my father wanted to sell the strip of land beside the road. A man from the district town had offered a good price for it, and my father talked about the money at dinner in the careful voice he used for things he had already decided. My grandmother said nothing. She cut her bread into small pieces and ate them slowly, and after the meal she went out to the bench in the dark, though there were no birds to call at that hour.

[5] The next morning she handed me the tin. I remember that it was warm from the sun and heavier than I expected, and that I nearly dropped it. "Shake it the way I do," she said. I shook it the way I thought she did. Nothing happened. The pigeons on the roof of the tower turned their heads and looked at me with their round orange eyes, the way people in a waiting room look at someone who has come through the wrong door.

[6] "Slower," she said. "You are not selling them anything."

[7] I tried again, slower, and made the clicking sound as well as I could. One bird came down, landed a little distance away and walked towards me sideways, as if it had come for some other reason entirely. Then another came, and then a rush of wings, and suddenly the ground around my feet was grey and moving. My grandmother laughed—a short, surprised laugh I had not heard from her in months.

[8] After that I fed the birds every morning before school, and on Fridays I climbed the narrow inside ladder to clean the pots while she called up instructions from below. She was strict. If I left old straw in a pot, she knew it by the way the birds behaved the next day. If I hurried, she told me to come down and begin again. When I complained to my mother, she said only that I should be glad my grandmother had found someone to be strict with.

[9] My father did not mention the land again that summer. I did not understand then that my mornings with the birds were part of an argument between him and his mother, an argument conducted without a single raised voice. I only knew that once, coming back from the tower with grain dust on my sleeves, I saw him standing at the gate, watching me. He looked at the tin, and at me, and then he went inside without a word.

[10] The tower still stands. I live in Cairo now, the pots are cracked, and a younger cousin feeds the birds when he remembers to. But when I visit, I take the tin down from its nail by the door and shake it slowly, and I wait, and they come.
questions.q: The passage is best described as the narrator's account of:
c: how she deliberately persuaded her father not to sell the family's land.
how she took over the care of her grandmother's pigeons during a summer when the family's land was at stake.
how her grandmother learned a clicking language from her own mother.
why she left the village and moved to Cairo as an adult.
questions.e: The narrator describes taking over the pigeons while her father wants to sell the land. A is too strong: in paragraph 9 she says she did not understand at the time that she was part of an argument, so she was not deliberately persuading anyone.
ce: Too strong: she says she 'did not understand then' that her mornings with the birds were part of an argument, so she did not set out to persuade anyone.
Right: the passage follows her learning to call and care for the birds while her father's plan to sell the land hangs over the family.
Too narrow: this is a single detail from paragraph 3, not what the whole passage is about.
Off target: the move to Cairo is mentioned in one line at the end and no reason is given.

Passage II — Social Science

SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about the history of the coffeehouse in Cairo. The historian quoted is fictional.

[1] Walk down almost any street in Cairo and you will pass an ahwa, a coffeehouse: a few tables spilling onto the pavement, the click of backgammon pieces, a waiter balancing a tray of small glasses, a television murmuring in the corner. The ahwa is so ordinary a part of the city that it is easy to forget it had a beginning. Yet for most of the city's history there was no such place, and when it first appeared, it was not welcomed by everyone.

[2] Coffee as a drink seems to have spread from Yemen, where in the fifteenth century members of Sufi orders took it up because it kept them awake during long night-time devotions. From there it travelled along trade and pilgrimage routes, and by the early sixteenth century it had reached Cairo, where students at the city's religious colleges were among its early drinkers.

[3] What was new was not only the drink but the place in which it was drunk. Before the coffeehouse, the main places where men met outside the home were the mosque, the market and the bathhouse, each with its own purpose and its own rules. The coffeehouse had no purpose except company. A man could enter, sit for as long as he liked for the price of a cup, and talk with people who were neither his relatives nor his business partners. "It was a room in which conversation itself was the reason for being there," writes the historian Karim Nassar. "That was genuinely new, and some people found it alarming."

[4] The alarm took several forms. Some religious scholars debated whether coffee was permitted at all, since it altered the drinker's state of mind, though most eventually concluded that it was. Others objected less to the drink than to the gatherings: idle talk, games and gossip, they argued, kept men from work and prayer. Rulers had their own worries. A room where strangers met to discuss the news was also a room where they might discuss their rulers. At various times and in various cities, coffeehouses were closed by order; each time, they reopened.

[5] Nassar argues that the coffeehouse survived because it answered a need that the older institutions could not. Cities like Cairo were growing, and more and more men lived and worked among people they had not grown up with. The coffeehouse offered a neutral ground where such people could become acquaintances. Over time, particular coffeehouses came to belong to particular groups: one served the workers of a certain trade, another the men from a certain village, another the students of a nearby school. A newcomer to the city could find, in the right ahwa, a piece of the place he had left.

[6] The coffeehouse also became a stage. In the nineteenth century, professional storytellers performed in Cairo's coffeehouses, reciting long tales over many evenings, and customers returned night after night to hear what happened next. Later, the radio took the storyteller's place, and crowds gathered in coffeehouses to listen to songs, speeches and football matches that few of them could have heard at home. In each period, the ahwa was where news and entertainment arrived first for people who could not afford them alone.

[7] Today the coffeehouse is changing again. Many young Cairenes meet in modern cafés with espresso machines and wireless internet, and women, who were long absent from the traditional ahwa, are now a common sight in these newer places and in some older ones. Nassar does not see this as the end of the coffeehouse but as one more chapter in its history. "The drinks change, the games change, the screens change," he writes. "What lasts is the idea of a room where you can sit among strangers and not be a stranger."

[8] That idea, he suggests, may be the coffeehouse's most important contribution to city life. Long before anyone spoke of "public opinion", the ahwa had made a place where ordinary people could form one.

Passage III — Humanities (Paired Passages)

HUMANITIES: Passage A is from an original essay by a calligrapher. Passage B is from an original essay by a designer of digital typefaces. Both writers are fictional.

PASSAGE A — "The Hand Remembers"

[1] My teacher did not let me write a single word for my first four months. I wrote only letters, and for most of that time only one letter: the alif, a single vertical stroke. Each morning I cut my reed pen, dipped it and drew the stroke down the page, again and again, while he sat beside me and shook his head. When at last he nodded, I understood that I had not been learning a letter. I had been learning a measurement.

[2] Classical Arabic calligraphy is built on proportion. In the tenth century, the scholar and official Ibn Muqla is credited with organising the main scripts around a single unit: the rhombic dot made by pressing the tip of the pen to the paper. The height of the alif is measured in dots, and the size of every other letter is measured against the alif. A calligrapher who has mastered these proportions can write a page in which every letter belongs to the same family.

[3] These proportions are not learned from a book. They are learned by copying a master's models, line by line, for years, until the hand knows what the eye alone cannot judge. That is why the tradition has always passed from teacher to student, and why a student who completes this training traditionally receives an ijaza, a licence from the teacher to sign his or her own work. The licence is not a certificate of knowledge. It is a statement that the student's hand can now be trusted.

[4] People sometimes ask me whether computers will make calligraphy unnecessary. I think the question misunderstands what calligraphy is. A font can reproduce the shapes of letters, but the shapes were never the whole art. The art lies in the small decisions a calligrapher makes while writing: how far to stretch a line so that a word fills its space, where to place one letter above another, when to let the pen run dry for a lighter stroke. A machine that offers me the same letter every time has removed exactly what I spent ten years learning.

PASSAGE B — "Letters That Move"

[1] Designing an Arabic typeface is harder than designing a Latin one, and the reason is the same thing that makes Arabic calligraphy beautiful: the letters are joined, and most of them change shape depending on whether they stand alone or come at the beginning, middle or end of a word. Early printing and computer systems often handled this badly. The type they produced was cramped and stiff, and many readers concluded that Arabic simply did not suit machines.

[2] That conclusion was wrong, but it was understandable. The first designers worked under technical limits that forced them to simplify. Today those limits have largely disappeared. A modern font can contain many forms of each letter, can choose between them according to the letters around it, and can stretch connecting strokes to fill a line, much as a calligrapher does by hand.

[3] I do not claim that a font is a calligrapher. A font makes choices according to rules that its designer wrote in advance; a calligrapher makes them in the moment. But this is a difference of situation rather than of value. Most Arabic that people read today appears in print or on screens: in messages, on signs, in schoolbooks. A child who learns to read from well-designed type learns letter shapes that carry the proportions of the classical scripts. A child who learns from poor type learns poor shapes.

[4] The best type designers I know have studied with calligraphers, and several are calligraphers themselves. They do not see their work as a replacement for the hand but as a way of carrying what the hand discovered into places the hand cannot reach. A calligrapher can write only a few pages a day. A good typeface, drawn once with care, can bring something of the same discipline to millions of pages.

Passage IV — Natural Science

NATURAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about the rock formations of Egypt's White Desert. The geologist quoted is fictional.

[1] At sunrise, the White Desert looks less like a desert than like a field of snow on which someone has set out a strange collection of sculptures. Across the floor of the Farafra Depression, in Egypt's Western Desert, white rock rises in shapes that visitors have named after whatever they resemble: mushrooms, chickens, camels, a tent. Some stand alone; others gather in groups like crowds at a bus stop. In the low light they glow pink and then gold before the midday sun bleaches them white again.

[2] The rock is chalk, and its whiteness is the first clue to its history. Chalk forms on the floor of a sea from the remains of countless tiny marine organisms whose shells and skeletons are made of calcium carbonate. Over very long periods, these remains settle in thick layers and harden into soft white rock. The chalk of the White Desert therefore tells geologists something that is hard to imagine when one stands in it today: tens of millions of years ago, this dry land lay beneath a sea.

[3] When the sea retreated and the land rose, the chalk was exposed to the weather, and for long periods that weather was wetter than today's. Water seeped into cracks and slowly dissolved parts of the rock, widening some gaps and leaving harder blocks standing between them. "Rain started the work," says the geologist Samir Hanna, who has studied the area for many years, "but wind finished it."

[4] Wind, in a desert, is not just moving air. It carries sand, and sand does the cutting. Most wind-blown sand grains do not fly high; they bounce along the ground in short hops, rarely rising more than a metre or so above the surface. As a result, the lower part of an exposed rock is struck far more often than its upper part. Over thousands of years, this steady blasting wears away the base of a pillar faster than its top. The strongest winds in the area blow from roughly the north.
The caps of the formations are usually harder than their stems.
The formations glow pink and gold in the low light.
questions.e: Paragraph 2 reasons from the chalk's marine origin to the ancient sea. C is a true detail, but it explains the shapes, not the sea.
ce: Right: paragraph 2 uses exactly this fact to conclude that 'this dry land lay beneath a sea'.
Wind direction tells us about today's weather, not about an ancient sea.
This explains the mushroom shape, not the origin of the rock.
Colour at sunrise is a visual effect, not evidence about the past.

questions.p:
Passage IV — Natural Science

NATURAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about the rock formations of Egypt's White Desert. The geologist quoted is fictional.

[1] At sunrise, the White Desert looks less like a desert than like a field of snow on which someone has set out a strange collection of sculptures. Across the floor of the Farafra Depression, in Egypt's Western Desert, white rock rises in shapes that visitors have named after whatever they resemble: mushrooms, chickens, camels, a tent. Some stand alone; others gather in groups like crowds at a bus stop. In the low light they glow pink and then gold before the midday sun bleaches them white again.

[2] The rock is chalk, and its whiteness is the first clue to its history. Chalk forms on the floor of a sea from the remains of countless tiny marine organisms whose shells and skeletons are made of calcium carbonate. Over very long periods, these remains settle in thick layers and harden into soft white rock. The chalk of the White Desert therefore tells geologists something that is hard to imagine when one stands in it today: tens of millions of years ago, this dry land lay beneath a sea.

[3] When the sea retreated and the land rose, the chalk was exposed to the weather, and for long periods that weather was wetter than today's. Water seeped into cracks and slowly dissolved parts of the rock, widening some gaps and leaving harder blocks standing between them. "Rain started the work," says the geologist Samir Hanna, who has studied the area for many years, "but wind finished it."

[4] Wind, in a desert, is not just moving air. It carries sand, and sand does the cutting. Most wind-blown sand grains do not fly high; they bounce along the ground in short hops, rarely rising more than a metre or so above the surface. As a result, the lower part of an exposed rock is struck far more often than its upper part. Over thousands of years, this steady blasting wears away the base of a pillar faster than its top. The outcome is the shape that gives the White Desert's most famous formations their name: a narrow stem holding up a wider cap.

[5] Hanna points out that the caps often survive for another reason as well. In many formations the top layer is a slightly harder rock than the chalk below it. "If you see a mushroom," he says, "look at the cap. It is almost always tougher than the stem. The wind cuts the soft rock and leaves the hard." Where no harder layer is present, the rock tends to wear down into low, rounded mounds instead of tall pillars.

[6] The direction of the wind matters too. In this part of the desert, the strongest and most frequent winds blow from roughly the north. Many formations are therefore streamlined: blunt and steep on the side that faces the wind and tapering away on the sheltered side, like the hull of a boat turned upside down. Geologists call such wind-shaped ridges yardangs, and the White Desert contains them at many sizes, from knee-high to the height of a house.

[7] The landscape is not finished. Each sandstorm removes a little more of every stem, and sooner or later each cap becomes too heavy for the narrowing rock beneath it and falls. Broken blocks scattered on the desert floor show where earlier mushrooms have already collapsed. Hanna estimates that some of the slender formations visitors photograph today will not survive more than a few centuries, though he admits that such estimates are uncertain. Meanwhile, new pillars are slowly being carved from the larger outcrops.

[8] For Hanna, this is what makes the place worth protecting. Vehicles that drive too close, and visitors who climb the formations or carve their names into the soft chalk, can damage in an afternoon what the wind took thousands of years to shape. "People think of rock as permanent," he says. "Here you can see that it is not. That is exactly why we should be careful with it."
questions.q: Hanna's claim in paragraph 8 that rock is not permanent is most directly supported by which detail from the passage?
c: 'In this part of the desert, the strongest and most frequent winds blow from roughly the north.'
'Samir Hanna, who has studied the area for many years'
'Broken blocks scattered on the desert floor show where earlier mushrooms have already collapsed.'
'Geologists call such wind-shaped ridges yardangs'
questions.e: The fallen blocks are observed evidence that rock changes. A is a true detail about wind direction, but it says nothing about rock changing over time.
ce: This is from paragraph 6 and describes wind direction, not change over time.
This is from paragraph 3 and tells us about Hanna, not about whether rock lasts.
Right: the fallen blocks are visible proof that the formations do not last for ever.
This is from paragraph 6 and only gives a name.

items: Read the reason for **every** answer choice, including the questions you got right: check that you chose the answer for the right reason.
Sort your wrong answers into Key Ideas and Details, Craft and Structure, and Integration of Knowledge and Ideas. The longest list is your weak skill.
Name the trap for each mistake: too extreme, too narrow, reversed, right detail but wrong person, or a dictionary meaning that does not fit the sentence.

Go back to the matching lessons: "Main Idea and Summary Questions", "Detail Questions", "Inference Questions", "Words and Phrases in Context", "Purpose, Function and Text Structure", "Point of View, Tone and Perspective" and "Paired Passages: Comparing Two Authors".
